lead: 16:8 time-restricted eating (TRE) is a daily meal-timing pattern in which all food is eaten within an eight-hour window, leaving sixteen hours of fasting that usually span the night plus part of the morning or evening. It is one variant of time-restricted eating, in which food is confined to a set daily window, commonly 8 to 12 hours.[1]

In looksmaxxing and wider fitness culture it is used mainly for leanness. Followers adopt it to lower body fat, to look more defined in the face and midsection, and to simplify eating routines by cutting the number of meals to plan. Some lifters pair it with a calorie surplus, using the window to fit large meals while still training hard.[3][13][14]

Published trials have studied the pattern in overweight adults, endurance runners and cyclists, dancers and resistance-trained lifters, generally in small groups over weeks to months.[2][3][4][5][7] Reviews describe the wider evidence on intermittent fasting as preliminary, with long-term effects not well studied and an advantage over ordinary calorie restriction that is limited.[1]

chain: Many people eat less overall and simplify meals
Lower body fat and a leaner, more defined look
angle.text: People use 16:8 as a structure for reducing calorie intake or for fitting a planned diet into fewer hours, aiming for lower body fat and sharper definition. Trials report changes in body composition and metabolic markers; studies of facial appearance under the pattern have not been published.

paras: Intermittent fasting is an umbrella term for schedules that alternate periods of fasting or markedly reduced intake with normal eating. Its main forms are alternate-day fasting, periodic fasting such as the 5:2 diet, and daily time-restricted eating.[1] Time-restricted eating differs from the other two in that it does not change which days are fasted but limits the hours of each day in which food is eaten. The 16:8 version is the best-known; stricter variants compress eating into one to two hours, as in one-meal-a-day plans.[1]

Some versions align the window with daylight hours, for example from after sunrise to around sunset, while others let the person choose a window that fits their schedule. A trial in middle-aged cyclists used a self-selected 16:8 window rather than a fixed clock time.[4][5] During the fast, practitioners typically allow water and unsweetened drinks such as coffee or tea; protocols differ on this and trials generally specify their own rules.

In fitness circles the pattern is often associated with the Leangains approach, a lifting-oriented version that popularised eating within a shortened daily window around training. Forum discussion treats 16:8 as the entry-level version of the idea and longer fasts as progressions from it.

Therapeutic fasting for obesity was studied as early as 1915, and interest revived in the 1960s after an enthusiastic report by Bloom and colleagues; early fasts lasted from one to fourteen days.[1] The 5:2 diet appeared in a 2011 article co-authored by Michelle Harvie and Mark Mattson, and Michael Mosley popularised it in the United Kingdom and Australia in 2012 through the BBC documentary Eat, Fast and Live Longer.[1]

Daily time-restricted eating gained a research profile through studies of circadian biology, which found that glucose metabolism and the hormone leptin follow a daily rhythm. Preliminary work has linked eating during the hours of melatonin secretion with higher glucose in young healthy adults.[1] Researchers describe meal timing as a potential new target for weight control, while stressing that the evidence is early.[1]

Intermittent fasting became a prominent diet trend in the late 2010s; a 2018 survey by the International Food Information Council ranked it the most popular diet that year, and it spread through Silicon Valley, celebrity endorsements and fitness media.[1] T Nation published articles on time-restricted feeding plans, including a 2016 piece titled The Time-Restricted-Plus Diet that discussed an eating window as a way to get and stay lean.[13][14]

The most direct route to fat loss is energy intake: with fewer hours available, many people eat fewer calories, although trials differ in whether participants were asked to count calories. In the seven-week Orthodox fasting comparison, the TRE arm followed a low-calorie 16/8 pattern, so intake restriction and timing were combined.[6]

Reviews describe additional proposed mechanisms. One is a metabolic switch: as fasting continues past the fed state (about four hours) and post-absorptive state, the body moves toward mobilising fat and using ketones, a transition described at roughly 12 to 36 hours of fasting, which a 16-hour fast may only partly reach.[1] Another is circadian alignment of food intake with the body's daily rhythm.[1] Studies of hormones such as irisin, nesfatin and lipolytic hormones in 16:8 groups explore these pathways.[7][8][9]

Reviews of intermittent fasting generally report weight loss of roughly 2.5 to 9.9 percent in adults with overweight or obesity, mostly fat mass with some lean-mass loss; for time-restricted eating, one summary reports a fat-to-lean loss ratio of about 4:1.[1] Cardiometabolic changes such as lower waist circumference, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting insulin are described as broadly similar to those seen with continuous calorie restriction, and the effect on blood pressure is smaller.[1]

Evidence that intermittent fasting outperforms ordinary calorie restriction for weight loss is described as limited.[1] A 2019 review cited dropout rates of 2 to 38 percent for intermittent fasting versus 0 to 50 percent for calorie restriction.[1]

Reviews also note that fasting before prolonged exercise lasting over 60 minutes reduces performance and that intermittent fasting does not appear to improve athletic performance in general.[1] Practitioners who train fasted or schedule workouts inside the window describe it differently, reporting that it suits their routines.[13][14]

Runners: an 8-week randomized trial in 23 male middle- and long-distance runners assigned 12 to 16:8 TRE and 11 to habitual eating while both continued habitual training. It measured body composition, energy and macronutrient intake, indices of endurance performance and metabolic health markers.[2]

Resistance-trained participants: 17 well-trained men (10) and women (7) were randomized to hypercaloric 16:8 TRE or a control pattern during supervised progressive resistance exercise four times a week. Both groups ate a 10 percent calorie surplus with 2.2 g per kg of daily protein, so the trial tested whether a restricted window affects muscle mass and strength under surplus conditions.[3]

Cyclists: studies in middle-aged male cyclists examined a self-selected 16:8 protocol and reported effects on fat oxidation, cardiometabolic markers and 10-km cycling performance in one report and cardiovascular markers in a quasi-experimental follow-up.[4][5]
Dancers: a study of female DanceSport dancers examined body composition and lipolytic hormones under 16/8 TRE.[7]

Overweight adults: in a study comparing a 7-week Orthodox religious fasting pattern (29 overweight adults) with a low-calorie 16/8 pattern (16 matched adults), both groups showed a trend toward weight loss at week 7 and measures were taken again six weeks after the diets ended.[6] Companion analyses from the same research program examined plasma irisin concentrations and nesfatin-related beta-cell function.[8][9]

Oral health: a three-arm trial of 66 healthy participants compared Bahai dry fasting, 16:8 TRE and a regular diet during experimentally induced gingivitis; the dry-fasting arm showed a smaller rise in gum bleeding than the other two arms.[10]

A 12-month randomized trial in adults with obesity compared a ketogenic diet with intermittent fasting on metabolic and orexin-A responses, and a real-world observational study in Chinese office workers tracked short-term BMI changes with self-selected diet patterns.[11][12]

Short-term effects reported for intermittent fasting include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired concentration, usually fading within about a month.[1] A 2018 systematic review found no major adverse effects, though reviews note that adverse effects have not been comprehensively studied.[1]

Health authorities and reviews advise against these diets for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, older adults, underweight people and people with or prone to eating disorders.[1] The US National Institute on Aging calls the research limited and inconclusive, the American Heart Association reports no good evidence of heart benefit, and the New Zealand Ministry of Health advises against it for people with diabetes.[1]

The pattern is discussed as a way to stay lean and reduce facial puffiness, often alongside calorie counting and lifting. Posters on T Nation describe the eating window as an easy-to-follow structure; the site's articles characterise modest time-restricted plans as working as well as stricter ones.[13][14] Published studies of facial appearance under TRE were not located; reported outcomes concern body composition and metabolic markers.

lore.intro: On lifting and fat-loss forums such as T Nation, 16:8 and related windows are discussed as simple tools for getting lean without elaborate meal planning.[13][14]

claims.claim: An eating window is an easy way to get lean.
claims.believers: Forum posters and T Nation authors describe a daily window as a simple tweak that helps people reduce intake and stay lean.[13][14]
claims.experts: Reviews report average weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent with intermittent fasting, broadly similar to continuous calorie restriction.[1]

claims.claim: Fasting preserves muscle while cutting fat.
claims.believers: Practitioners who lift describe keeping strength while leaning out within a window.[13]
claims.experts: A review summary reports a fat-to-lean loss ratio of about 4:1 for time-restricted eating, and a trial in trained lifters tested a restricted window during a calorie surplus.[1][3]

claims.claim: A shorter window reduces facial puffiness.
claims.believers: Some users report a leaner, less puffy face when they follow the window.
claims.experts: Published studies examine body composition and metabolic markers; none located has measured facial appearance.[2][6]

claims.claim: Longer or stricter windows work better than 16:8.
claims.believers: Some posters progress to one meal a day, while T Nation authors have described modest windows as working as well as stricter ones.[14]
claims.experts: Reviews describe the evidence on specific window lengths as preliminary, with long-term effects not well studied.[1]

name: 16:8 time-restricted eating

card.summary: Eat inside an eight-hour window and fast the other sixteen; the research is about weight and metabolic markers, not looks.
card.note: Not advised for pregnancy, adolescents, or people with eating-disorder histories.

quick.overview:
16:8 time-restricted eating means eating all meals within eight hours and fasting for sixteen. It is popular for fat loss and a leaner look.

Trials are small and short, mostly in overweight adults and athletes, and reviews report weight loss broadly similar to ordinary calorie restriction.
quick.mechanism: The window limits when food is eaten, which for many people reduces total calorie intake; researchers also study effects on fat oxidation and metabolic hormones.
quick.risks: Reported short-term effects include hunger, irritability, headaches and poor concentration. Reviews advise against it for pregnancy, youth, underweight people and those with eating disorders.
